0.title: Held Fast Through the Fire
0.essay:
Suffering is not optional Christianity. The New Testament does not promise believers a life free from pain. It promises the presence of a God who enters pain, redeems it, and will one day end it.

Take heart

Jesus told his disciples plainly, “In the world you will have tribulation.” Then he added the words that change everything: “But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Unprepared

The church in the comfortable West has often been poorly prepared for suffering. We have preached a gospel whose benefits are real but whose costs we have played down. We have built worship cultures geared to celebration rather than lament. And many Christians are genuinely surprised when hardship comes, and assume it means something has gone wrong — with their faith, with God’s goodness, or with the world’s fairness. None of these conclusions is biblical.

For the person in the furnace

This study is written for the person in the furnace, and for those who stand alongside them. The “God of all comfort” (2 Corinthians 1:3) does not explain all suffering in this life. But he does accompany it, with his presence, his word, his people and the certain hope of resurrection. That is enough. It is more than enough.

The chapters

The Theology of Suffering: why God allows it. Lament: the biblical language of pain. Suffering and Sanctification: what God is doing in the fire. The Sovereignty of God: the anchor in the storm. Community and Suffering: bearing one another’s burdens. And The Hope of Glory: the horizon that changes everything.

For reflection

When suffering has come to you, what did you assume it meant? Bring that honestly to God as you begin.

1.title: The Theology of Suffering: Why God Allows It
1.essay:
If God is all-powerful and all-good, why does he allow his children to suffer? For the suffering believer this is not an abstract puzzle. It is a cry from a hospital room, a graveside, or a sleepless night.

Several answers, held together

The Bible does not give one neat answer. It gives several partial answers, held together, which the suffering person needs to hold in hand at once.

First, suffering is not what God originally intended. It is the consequence of the fall, the shape the world takes when it is disordered by sin. Paul writes that “the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22). Pain, disease, disaster and death are not the world as God designed it, but the world as human rebellion has distorted it. So suffering is not necessarily God’s specific judgment on the sufferer. When people asked Jesus about those killed when a tower fell, he asked, “do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem?” (Luke 13:4). Of a man born blind, he said, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him” (John 9:3).

Second, God is not absent from suffering. He entered it in the incarnation, bore it on the cross, and transformed it in the resurrection.

Third, God works purposefully through suffering. Scripture names many purposes: testing and strengthening faith (James 1:2–4), producing character (Romans 5:3–5), shaping us into Christ’s likeness (Philippians 3:10), equipping us to comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:3–4), displaying his power in our weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9–10), and sometimes fatherly discipline (Hebrews 12:5–11). No single purpose explains all suffering. Wisdom discerns which are at work in a particular case.

Fourth, there is mystery. Some suffering in this life will receive no explanation in this life. An honest pastor admits this, and does not rush to fill the silence with premature comfort.

The cross at the centre

The cross is the centre of a Christian understanding of suffering. God did not watch human suffering from a distance. He entered it. The Son of God, who could have been exempt from every human pain, took the form of a servant and walked the road to Calvary. He cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46).

The cross does not resolve the problem of evil like a philosophical proof. It addresses it personally. God has been inside the darkest suffering and was not destroyed by it. He is trustworthy precisely because he did not exempt himself from what he asks his people to endure. The suffering Christian is not alone in the fire.

You will have tribulation

Jesus does not promise exemption. He promises his presence and his victory. In the world, tribulation — not possibly, not only for the unlucky, but certainly. And then: “I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). The victory is already won. The Christian lives in both at once: in the tribulation, and in the One who has overcome it.

Through, not around

God promised Israel, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you” (Isaiah 43:2). Notice the word: through, not around. God does not promise to keep his people away from the waters and the fire. He promises to be with them in it.

A Christian who expects God to take them around suffering will be disappointed. One who expects God to be present through it will find the promise kept. When Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego came out of Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace, “no smell of fire had come upon them” (Daniel 3:27). And a fourth figure had walked with them in the flames.

Not worth comparing

“For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18). Paul writes as a man who had been beaten, shipwrecked, imprisoned and left cold and hungry. He is not saying the sufferings are small. He is saying the glory is so vast that the comparison collapses.

Elsewhere he calls his sufferings “light momentary affliction” that “is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). Glory has weight. And the affliction is doing something, right now. The eternal perspective does not make the pain feel less. It makes it mean more.

It is well

Horatio Spafford lost his four daughters when their ship sank in the Atlantic. He sailed to join his grieving wife in Europe, and the story is told that, near the place where his daughters died, he wrote: “When peace like a river attendeth my way, when sorrows like sea billows roll; whatever my lot, thou hast taught me to say, it is well, it is well with my soul.” That is not denial. It is trust in the God who is sovereign over the sea, even when the sea has taken everything.

Joni Eareckson Tada was left paralysed by a diving accident at seventeen. Over more than fifty years she has become one of the most thoughtful voices on disability, suffering and God’s sovereignty. Her testimony is that God’s purposes in her suffering have been richer than anything her earlier life was producing. It is not a minimising of pain, but a magnifying of grace.

For reflection

Which of the four answers above do you most need to hold on to right now? What difference does it make that God walks with you through the fire, not merely around it?

2.title: Lament: The Biblical Language of Pain
2.essay:
One of the greatest gifts the church can give its suffering members is permission to lament. A large part of the Psalter, the prayer book of Israel and the church, is made up of raw, honest, sometimes angry cries to God.

No words for pain

A Christian culture that has lost lament has produced a spirituality that works only in seasons of health and blessing. When suffering comes, the person who has never learned to lament has no words for their pain and no permission to be honest. They must either perform a faith they do not feel, or step outside the bounds of their church to find their grief acknowledged.

Faith under pressure

Lament is not the absence of faith. It is faith under pressure, speaking honestly. “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). The psalmist who cries like this is not abandoning God. They are bringing their pain into the relationship, addressing it to God, and refusing to resolve it too quickly. That is more faithful than bright reassurance that tries to skip from suffering straight to praise without passing through the darkness.

The shape of lament

Most lament psalms follow a pattern. They address God by name. They complain, describing the situation honestly. They petition, asking God to act. They express trust, affirming his character in the darkness. And often they end with a vow of praise, looking ahead to rescue. The move from complaint to trust is not automatic. It is a deliberate act of faith, returning to what is known about God even when what is felt says otherwise.

Jesus prayed it

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?” (Psalm 22:1). Jesus died with this psalm on his lips. The One who had lived in unbroken communion with the Father experienced a forsakenness no one else has known. By quoting Psalm 22, he placed his suffering within the lament tradition, and he ensures that a Christian who prays it in their own darkness prays it with him.

And notice: the cry is still addressed. My God. Even when God seems silent, he is still the God to whom we cry. Jesus is the great lamenter, and those who pray the laments share “his sufferings” (Philippians 3:10), and with them his resurrection.

The psalm that ends in darkness

Psalm 88 is the only psalm that never turns to praise. “But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you. O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 88:13–14). Its last line is “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18).

That psalm exists to give the person in the deepest, unresolved suffering a prayer they can pray, one that does not require them to manufacture faith, hope or praise they cannot honestly offer. God inspired it, and preserved it. He has made room in Scripture for the one who has not yet turned the corner. The church must make room for them too. They are not outside the community of faith; they are in its longest night, and morning will come.

But this I call to mind

Lamentations was written in the ruins of Jerusalem. “Remember my affliction and my wanderings, the wormwood and the gall!” (Lamentations 3:19). The poet does not deny the bitterness. Then comes the turn: “But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases” (Lamentations 3:21–22).

He holds the reality of the suffering in one hand, and then deliberately calls to mind the love of God. That is not wishful thinking. It is the discipline of faith: choosing to remember what is true about God when circumstances argue otherwise.

How long? in heaven

Even the martyrs before God’s throne cry out, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long?” (Revelation 6:10). Lament is not left behind at death; it is brought into God’s very presence. It is a faithful response to the gap between what God has promised and what has not yet arrived. God receives the cry, gives comfort, and promises that the answer is coming.

Job and Jeremiah

Job is the Bible’s great extended lament. He cursed the day of his birth (Job 3), argued his case, demanded a hearing, and rejected his friends’ glib comfort: “miserable comforters are you all” (Job 16:2). And God did not rebuke Job for lamenting. He rebuked the friends: “you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:7). Honest, searching lament pleases God more than the tidy reassurances of people who are not suffering.

Jeremiah’s laments are some of the most anguished poetry in Scripture. “O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived” (Jeremiah 20:7). It is the cry of a man at the end of his resources. God did not abandon him. These cries are in the Bible as permission, and as company, for our own dark hours.

For reflection

Have you ever felt you had to hide your pain from God or from your church? Try praying Psalm 13 or Psalm 88 this week, in your own words, honestly.

3.title: Suffering and Sanctification: What God Is Doing in the Fire
3.essay:
Suffering is not only something the Christian endures until it is over. It is something God is doing. Scripture is remarkably consistent: in the hands of God, suffering is a refining fire.

Not tidy lessons

That does not mean every trial has a clear lesson attached. The mystery of suffering resists tidy explanation. But it does mean God is never passive in his children’s suffering. He is always working, always attending, always forming. The Christian in the fire is not forgotten; they are being refined.

So the most important question in suffering may not be “Why is this happening?” That may not be answered in this life. A more fruitful question is “How do I cooperate with what God is doing in this?” That question leads somewhere: to prayer, to Scripture, to the church, to the practices that keep the soul turned towards God when everything presses against it.

Count it all joy

“Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing” (James 1:2–4).

James does not say feel joy. He says count it joy, an act of the mind, reframing the experience by what we know. And what we know is that trials produce steadfastness: the strength to remain under pressure without collapsing. Character cannot be downloaded; it must be formed. Trials are the forming pressure.

Paul says the same: “we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame” (Romans 5:3–5).

Gold in the fire

Peter writes, “though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of your faith — more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire — may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:6–7).

Gold ore entering a refiner’s fire contains impurities. The fire burns away the dross and leaves the gold purer, more precious, more itself. Tested faith is the same. The fire burns away the shallow, the performed and the assumed, and leaves something genuine: trust that holds because it has been pressed.

Conformed to Christ

God has predestined his people “to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). And his Son was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). The path to his likeness passes through suffering. Not because suffering is good in itself, but because what it produces — humility, compassion, dependence on God, loosened grip on worldly security — are the marks of the crucified Christ.

Paul treated sharing Christ’s sufferings not as something to minimise but as part of his deepest goal: “that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death” (Philippians 3:10). The kingdom’s pattern is down before up, death before resurrection, cross before crown. The suffering Christian is not on a detour from the road to glory. They are on it, and Christ’s footprints mark the way ahead.

Stripped of self-sufficiency

One of suffering’s most consistent effects is to strip away self-sufficiency. The healthy, comfortable, successful person can keep up the illusion that they are managing their own life, with God as a supplement. Suffering destroys that illusion. It drives us to prayer, to the church, to Scripture, to the desperate dependence on God that is in fact the normal and right condition of a creature before its Creator.

Comforted to comfort

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

Comfort flows from God to the sufferer, and from the sufferer to others. Someone who has received God’s comfort in their own affliction carries something no training can supply: the credibility of one who has been there, the authority of one who has found God faithful in the dark, and a heart broken open to others’ pain. The God who allows suffering also turns it into ministry.

The fire produced gold

Fanny Crosby was blinded as a baby, reportedly through a doctor’s mistake. She wrote thousands of hymns, and refused to let her blindness become a source of bitterness. She is reported to have said she was glad, because the first face she would ever see would be the face of Jesus. Her suffering produced not bitterness but extraordinary fruitfulness.

C. S. Lewis wrote The Problem of Pain as a healthy scholar, an able defence of why God permits suffering. Twenty years later, after his wife Joy died of cancer, he wrote A Grief Observed, a raw account of what grief feels like from the inside. He discovered that the God he had defended so ably was also the God who walked with him through the most disorienting grief of his life.

For reflection

Instead of asking only “Why is this happening?”, what would it look like to ask “How do I cooperate with what God is doing in this?” Whom might God be preparing you to comfort?

4.title: The Sovereignty of God: The Anchor in the Storm
4.essay:
The sovereignty of God is not abstract philosophy. It is the anchor of the suffering Christian.

If God were not sovereign

If God were not sovereign over suffering — if cancer, bereavement, addiction and injustice lay outside his rule — then prayer for relief would be pointless, trust in his goodness would be misplaced, and the sufferer would be ultimately alone in the universe. But if nothing happens outside his knowledge and governance, then suffering, however devastating, is not the last word. It is a word within a larger story that God is writing towards a good end.

Sovereign and loving

The pastoral challenge is to present God’s sovereignty not as cold comfort that explains everything away, but as the warm assurance that the God who rules all things is the Father who loves his children, the Shepherd who carries his lambs, the High Priest who sympathises with our weakness. In the God of the Bible, sovereignty and love are not in tension. They meet in the One who is both King of the universe and the Lamb who was slain.

All things work together

“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). This is one of the most precious and most misused texts in Scripture. Precious, because it says nothing — not cancer, bereavement, betrayal or loss — lies outside God’s governance or beyond his redeeming reach.

But read it carefully. It does not say everything is good. It says everything works together for good, and that is God’s work, not ours. And the good is defined by the next verse: to be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). The sufferer is not promised comfort now, but formation now and glory then. It is not a slogan to throw at a grieving friend. It is a rock to stand on.

And it rests on the cross: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

You meant evil; God meant good

Joseph was sold into slavery by his brothers and spent some thirteen years as a slave and prisoner before God’s purposes became visible. When at last he faced his brothers, he said, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Genesis 50:20).

That is a whole theology of suffering in a sentence. Two intentions, one event. The brothers’ evil was real, and God did not excuse it. But God governed through it, not around it. The same actions that were wicked on their part were instruments of his saving purpose.

Reformed theology distinguishes between God’s decree — what he has determined will happen — and his commands — what he tells his creatures to do. That lets us affirm both that God governs all things, and that he is not the author of sin and does not approve evil. Joseph’s words are the classic biblical expression of that mystery.

Now my eye sees you

Job is the Bible’s most sustained engagement with sovereignty and suffering. He demanded an explanation, and never received one. God’s answer from the whirlwind did not explain Job’s suffering; it revealed the majesty and wisdom of the One who governs all things. And Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42:5).

Hearing about God and seeing God are different kinds of knowledge, and the second is far more transforming. Job’s suffering did not produce a satisfying theory. It produced a transformed knowledge of God. The Christian who cries out for an explanation may receive instead what Job received: not understanding, but encounter. That is the greater gift.

Trust with all your heart

“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths” (Proverbs 3:5–6). All your heart, all your ways, including the suffering. A sufferer sees partially, temporarily, and through the distorting lens of pain. God sees the whole, eternally, with perfect wisdom.

A Christian who demands an explanation before they will trust has put their own understanding above God’s wisdom. The wiser path is to trust his character — his goodness, wisdom, love and power — even when circumstances make no sense.

No pit so deep

Corrie ten Boom and her family hid Jews from the Nazis in occupied Holland. She and her sister Betsie were sent to Ravensbrück concentration camp, where Betsie died. Corrie carried Betsie’s words for the rest of her life: “There is no pit so deep that he is not deeper still.” Those words were not the product of comfortable theology, but of God’s faithfulness proved in the worst place the twentieth century produced.

For reflection

Where are you tempted to lean on your own understanding of your circumstances? How does Genesis 50:20 help you trust God with what you cannot yet see?

5.title: Community and Suffering: Bearing One Another's Burdens
5.essay:
Suffering is not meant to be endured alone. The church is not a collection of individuals who happen to share a building on Sunday, but a body in which the pain of one member is the pain of all.

Suffering in secret

“If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together” (1 Corinthians 12:26). That is how the body actually works when it functions as God designed.

The tragedy of much church life is that people suffer alone. The public face of the congregation is healthy, smiling and self-sufficient. The private reality of many members is grief, anxiety, chronic illness, marriage trouble, debt and depression, hidden behind a Sunday performance because the culture of the church does not make room for honesty. That is a failure of the body to be a body.

Two convictions

Recovering real community around suffering begins with two convictions. First, honesty about pain is not a failure of faith but an expression of it. Second, presence matters more than words.

The friend who turns up and stays, who asks the unglamorous questions and listens to the answers, who brings a meal and sits in the silence, is worth more than the friend who sends a theological explanation by text. Job’s friends were right for seven days, when they sat with him in the dust and said nothing. They went wrong when they started explaining.

Bear one another’s burdens

“Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). The word means heavy loads, the kind no one can carry alone. Every church contains people carrying such loads, often invisibly. The command is to see them, to step into their situation and to share the weight.

That is not an extraordinary act reserved for crises. It is the normal texture of Christian community. And it fulfils the law of the One who said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Weep with those who weep

“Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). The second command is harder. Celebrating with others comes naturally. Weeping with them means deliberately entering pain that is not our own.

The temptation is to cut the weeping short: to move quickly to comfort, to explanation, to the silver lining, because sitting with grief is uncomfortable. But a person in acute suffering rarely needs to be reminded that God is in control. They need someone to enter their pain, to acknowledge how terrible it is, and to weep. The theology can come later, after the tears. Jesus, who knew he was about to raise Lazarus, still wept at his tomb.

Body or audience?

Paul’s picture of the body has immediate consequences. A healthy body does not ignore a broken bone and hope it heals. The whole body reorganises around the injury. A church that has truly become a body will not leave a grieving family to grieve alone, the chronically ill to manage alone, or the depressed to sink alone. When one member’s child dies, everyone grieves. When one member receives a cancer diagnosis, everyone mobilises. The question for every congregation is: are we a body, or an audience?

Confession and prayer

“Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). James links healing with community practices, not private ones. A suffering person who brings their fears, doubts and needs into the fellowship, and receives its prayer, draws on a resource that isolation cannot give. Every church has this resource. The question is whether its culture makes it available to those who need it most.

Practical love

The New Testament’s commands about suffering members are relentlessly practical: visit the sick (Matthew 25:36), care for widows (James 1:27), pray for the sick (James 5:14–15), restore the fallen (Galatians 6:1). None of these is first a programme. They are acts of personal love, one member serving another in the details of their need: a meal, a lift to the hospital, an afternoon of childcare, a regular phone call.

Staying when it costs

Christianity spread rapidly in the Roman Empire partly because of the church’s care for the suffering: the sick, the destitute, the abandoned and the dying. When plague swept through cities, many fled. Christians often stayed and nursed the sick, pagans included. Their willingness to stay when staying was costly was a powerful testimony to the gospel.

Many pastors observe that some of the most powerful care is given by the person who simply comes and stays, without answers, sitting in the hospital room, holding a hand and praying. The sufferer who receives this is receiving something of the incarnation: God with us, not solving the problem, but entering it.

For reflection

Is your church more like a body or an audience? Who in your fellowship is carrying a heavy load, and what is one practical thing you could do for them this week?

6.title: The Hope of Glory: The Eschatological Horizon
6.essay:
The final and greatest resource for the suffering Christian is hope: not optimism, but the certain expectation of what God has promised, grounded in what he has already done in Christ.

Not optimism

Optimism is a temperament, a tendency to expect things to turn out well. Christian hope is different. It rests on the resurrection of Jesus. The resurrection proves that death does not have the final word, and if death does not, neither does suffering.

Paul is blunt: “If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied” (1 Corinthians 15:19). A suffering Christian whose hope stops at the edge of this life is suffering without the gospel’s greatest resource.

Groaning in hope

Romans 8 describes three groanings: creation groaning, believers groaning, and the Spirit groaning. “And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26).

Groaning is not a failure of faith. It is the sound of hope. The Spirit we have already received makes us long for the full harvest: the redemption of the body and the completion of our adoption. And every groan is heading towards a resolution as certain as the resurrection that guarantees it.

The tent and the building

“For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1). The tent is temporary and fragile, exposed to the storms of illness and age. The building is eternal and solid.

A person whose body is failing through illness or age is not losing everything. They are losing the tent. The building is being prepared. That knowledge does not remove the pain, but it changes how it is carried: the tent does not need to last for ever.

To die is gain

Paul wrote to the Philippians from prison, chained to a Roman guard and facing possible execution. And he wrote, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). And again, “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11).

Every remaining day of life is for Christ. And death is not mere relief from pain, but gain: more of Christ, face to face. Those are not the words of a man in denial, but of a man whose hope reached beyond his circumstances. Such a person is not brave because they are naturally fearless. They are secure because death itself has been conquered. “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55). “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

Every tear

Revelation gives the suffering Christian their final orientation. “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4).

It is the most tender picture in all of Scripture’s hope: God himself, with his own hand, wiping away every tear. Not sending an angel or issuing a decree. Every tear wept in every sorrow of human history is known to him, and will be wiped away by him. The word anymore marks the end: death, mourning, crying and pain are finished.

All things new

Then the One on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5). Not “all new things,” replacing the old creation, but “all things new,” renewing the creation that is. The world that has groaned under the curse will be renewed, not abandoned. Bodies wasted by illness will be raised. Relationships broken by death will be restored. And God’s people will live in that renewed world in resurrection bodies, for ever.

Already and not yet

The New Testament holds two truths together. The kingdom has already come, in Christ’s resurrection, in the Spirit’s presence, and in the new birth of believers. And it has not yet come in its fullness: we still suffer, groan and die. The suffering Christian lives in the not-yet. But the already is real. The firstfruits of the Spirit are truly tasted now, and they are the guarantee of the full harvest to come.

The last door

Vibia Perpetua, a young mother martyred in Carthage in AD 203, kept a prison diary in the days before her death. In it she recorded a vision of the life to come that gave her courage to face the arena. The hope of glory did not make death easy. It made it bearable. It turned the last enemy into the last door.

For reflection

What would change in how you carry your present suffering if you truly believed Revelation 21:4? Picture the moment God wipes your tears away, and bring that hope into today.
